newsitem.title: USA: Dlr/mark hits highs by US noon as equities recover.
newsitem.headline: Dlr/mark hits highs by US noon as equities recover.

text.p: Dollar traders got caught short as a feared breakdown in U.S. equity markets failed to transpire, lifting the dollar against the mark and triggering stop-loss buy orders, dealers said.
Dealers set up short dollar positions as U.S. stock markets took a dive at the open, led by a slide in high-tech shares after Intel Corp said its second quarter earnings would be below expectations.
However, the equity market cut its losses before midday and the dollar shot up to a session high of 1.7093 marks

"It's stop-loss buying. People started to sell (dollars) as the perception was that the stock market would sell heavily," said John Nelson, foreign exchange trading manager at ABN-AMRO Bank in Chicago.
"The market got short and we've just broken 1.7040/50 which is a major resistance area. (Dollar/mark) will trade higher, probably up to 1.7120," he added.
The dollar rose to 1.7085/90 by midday from 1.7010/15 at the open, but slipped to 116.36/41 yen from 116.40/45.

Fears of a meltdown in equities stole the spotlight from a mixed bag of U.S. economic data releases, pro-dollar remarks by New York Federal Reserve President William McDonough and a verbal standoff between German government and central bank officials over Bonn's controversial plan to revalue Bundesbank gold.
And crucial events set for Sunday -- the French second-round election and a reported meeting of German Chancellor Helmut Kohl's cabinet -- kept dealers from establishing dollar views.
The dollar fell after the Commerce Department reported its second estimate for first quarter GDP growth at 5.8 percent compared to a previously released 5.6 percent expansion rate.
The figure disappointed dealers expecting a revised figure of at least 6.0 percent, as forecast in a Reuters survey.

The University of Michigan's final index of consumer sentiment for May rose to 103.2 compared to 101.4 in April while the Chicagoland Business Barometer fell to a seasonally adjusted 56.8 in May from 57.2 in April. April new home sales fell 7.7 percent -- the sharpest rate drop in six months, the Commerce Department said.

"It's Friday and end-of-month, so I don't think anyone really wants to go out on a limb today given the fact that we've got a lot more important numbers coming out next week," said a currency analyst at a U.S. investment bank.

Meanwhile, German Finance Minister Theo Waigel said the government's plan to revalue Bundesbank gold reserves was not an attack of the central bank's independence and that he's willing to talk at anytime with the Bundesbank about the plan.
However, markets remained skeptic and his insistence that the revaluation law will pass parliament by summer failed to raise positive market sentiment for the dollar.

Bundesbank council member Reimut Jochimsen said the central bank's council is "determined" on the gold issue but that there are no plans for resignations. He also said the market and public do not yet appreciate the full impact of the plan and that the Bundesbank may consider partial reserve revaluation in 1998 after EMU membership has been decided.
The analyst said the conflict in Germany sparked a conflict of opinion in the currency markets.

"It increases one of two alternatives -- an EMU delay or a soft EMU and those mean different things for the dollar against Europe so people don't know quite which way to jump," the currency expert said.
In other trading, the dollar rose to 1.4148/58 Swiss francs from 1.4100/07 and slipped to Canadian $1.3803/08 from C$1.3824/29. Sterling slipped to $1.6350/60 from 1.6378/88.
